Frequently Asked Questions How does hydroelectric power work step by step? Water is stored at a height behind a dam or diverted from a river. It flows down a sealed pipe called a penstock, gaining speed and pressure. The moving water spins a turbine, the turbine shaft turns a generator, and the generator produces electricity through electromagnetic induction. A transformer raises the voltage for the power lines, and the water flows back into the river below the plant. What type of energy does hydroelectric power use? It starts with gravitational potential energy, the energy water has because it is raised above the turbine. As the water falls, that becomes kinetic energy. The turbine turns it into rotational kinetic energy, and the generator turns the rotation into electrical energy. Ultimately the energy came from the Sun, which evaporated the water and lifted it to high ground as rain or snow. Is hydroelectric power renewable? Yes. The first is how much water flows each second. The second is how far it falls. A huge river with a short drop and a thin stream with a very tall drop can both make plenty of power. The generator does the final step. Inside it, magnets spin past coils of wire, and that motion pushes electric charges along the wire. So the chain is simple: height, then speed, then spin, then electricity. How Does a Hydroelectric Dam Work? A conventional hydro plant follows the same path every time the water moves through it: - Store. A dam blocks a river and builds up a reservoir. The water surface now sits far above the river below the dam. - Intake. Gates near the bottom of the reservoir open, and screens keep out logs and debris. - Penstock. The water rushes down a large sealed pipe called a penstock. It loses height and gains speed and pressure. - Turbine. The water strikes or flows through curved blades and sets the turbine shaft spinning.

A study led by the National Laboratory of the Rockies on hydropower flexibility found that the firm capacity, the guaranteed minimum amount of electric power a facility will be able to deliver, of U.S. hydropower facilities is estimated to be over 24 GW. This is enough to power between 16 to 24 million homes. To replace this capability with storage would require the construction of 24 GW of 10-hour storage facilities. Not only does this amount of storage—outside of hydropower facilities— not exist in the United States today but adding them to the grid could be costly and time consuming. How Does Hydropower Work? Hydropower technologies generate power by leveraging elevation differences. This is usually created by a dam or diversion structure that interrupts the flow of water in a river. The Department of Energy's "Hydropower 101" video explains how hydropower works and highlights some of the research and development efforts of the Hydropower and Hydrokinetic Office (H2O) in this area. The water cycle, driven by sunlight, keeps refilling rivers and reservoirs, so the energy source does not run out the way coal or natural gas does. Hydropower can still be limited locally by long droughts, by silt slowly filling reservoirs, and by the shrinking number of good river sites that have not already been dammed. How efficient is hydroelectric power? Large modern hydro turbines and generators usually convert about 85 to 92 percent of the water's available energy into electricity. That is far higher than fuel-burning power plants, which lose most of their energy as waste heat. Small plants and older equipment tend to be somewhat less efficient, often in the 60 to 80 percent range. What are the main disadvantages of hydroelectric power? Building a large dam is very costly and can take years. The reservoir may flood farmland, forests and towns, forcing people to move. Dams block fish migration and change water temperature and sediment downstream. In dry years output can fall sharply, and new reservoirs can release methane from decaying plants. Key Facts - Hydroelectric power converts the gravitational potential energy of water into electricity using a turbine and a generator. - The power of a hydro plant is about P = ηρgQh, so it rises in proportion to both the flow rate and the head. - Large modern hydro turbines convert roughly 85 to 92 percent of the water's energy into electricity. - Pumped storage plants store surplus electricity by pumping water uphill and return about 70 to 80 percent of it later. - Hydropower supplies about 15 percent of the world's electricity and is the largest renewable source of it. - The generator inside every hydro plant works by electromagnetic induction, discovered by Michael Faraday in 1831. - Hydro plants can change output within minutes, which helps balance grids that also use wind and solar power. Water wheels ground grain and drove sawmills for centuries before anyone had heard of electricity. A modern hydro plant does the same basic job with far better engineering: a carefully shaped turbine, a sealed steel pipe and a generator that can feed a national grid. Hydropower is a renewable energy source because the Sun keeps lifting water back uphill for free. Sunlight evaporates water from oceans and lakes, the vapor rises and cools, and rain or snow falls on high ground. Rivers then carry it back down, and a hydro plant takes a share of that energy on the way. Hydroelectric Power Explained Simply Picture a bucket of water on a high shelf. If you tip it over a small paddle wheel, the falling water pushes the paddles around. Now imagine the shelf is a mountain lake and the paddle wheel is the size of a house. Actually, hydroelectric and coal-fired power plants produce electricity using similar mechanisms. In both cases a power source is used to turn a propeller-like piece called a turbine, which then turns a metal shaft in an electric generator, which is the motor that produces electricity. A coal-fired power plant burns coal to heat water and turn it into steam to turn the turbine blades; whereas a hydroelectric plant uses falling water to turn the turbine. passages.text: At a Glance Hydroelectric power is electricity made from moving water: water drops through a height called the head, spins a turbine, and the turbine turns a generator. The power available is about P = η ρ g Q h, where η is efficiency, ρ is water density, g is gravitational acceleration, Q is the flow rate and h is the head. More water or a bigger drop means more power. - Energy source Gravitational potential energy of water (PE = mgh) - Power formula P = η ρ g Q h (watts) - Main parts Reservoir or intake, penstock, turbine, generator, transformer - Typical efficiency About 85–92% for large modern turbines - Renewable? Yes, the water cycle refills rivers and reservoirs - Depends on Flow rate and head (height the water falls) What Is Hydroelectric Power? Hydroelectric power, often shortened to hydropower, is electricity produced from water that moves downhill. The water is guided through a turbine on its way down, and the spinning turbine drives a generator. Nothing is burned, so the plant itself releases no smoke or exhaust while it runs. The idea is old.
